title: Swarms should show the same cognitive illusions as vertebrate brains

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Swarms should show the same cognitive illusions as vertebrate brains

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The proposed scale-invariant scaling of cognition predicts that swarm organisms should fall prey to the same kinds of cognitive illusions and failures of rationality as vertebrate brains, which the author says has been observed in ants and slime molds.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Levin M 2019, The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition › The Agent’s Evolutionary Back-Story: Scaling of Information by Bioelectricity

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: A prediction of this proposed scaling is that swarm organisms should fall prey to the same kinds of cognitive illusions and specific failures of rationality as do vertebrate brains, which has indeed been observed in ants and slime molds (Sakiyama and Gunji, 2013, 2016; Tani et al., 2014; Beekman and Latty, 2015).

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Levin M, “The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition”, Frontiers in psychology (2019), doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02688; section “The Agent’s Evolutionary Back-Story: Scaling of Information by Bioelectricity”. Scope: Swarm and collective organisms (ants, slime molds) compared with vertebrate brains

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2019-boundary-19: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.56

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Specific choice anomalies and rational benchmarks are measurable, and published behavioral datasets cover some taxa. Existing observations can test examples but not the broad prediction of the same kinds of illusions across swarm organisms.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Apply matched decision tasks that instantiate named biases to ants, slime molds, and vertebrates, and compare whether deviations from an explicit rational benchmark have the same qualitative signature.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Tasks are difficult to equate across species and collectives.

Similar aggregate errors can arise from different mechanisms.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction is comparative behavior on shared tasks, and the paper says ants and slime molds already show the failures. Those results are published measurements that a reviewer can compile, and they are not a downloadable dataset with official trial files. The overlap is a handful of paradigms, so the scope 'the same kinds of illusions' is only sampled. Mechanism differences keep the compilation suggestive. No repository is listed because none holds the choice-level data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Match named illusions or rationality failures (choice paradoxes, Weber-like biases) between a vertebrate paradigm and the same paradigm in ants and in slime molds, using choice frequencies. Shared failure modes support the scaling prediction; systematic success of the collectives on tasks where vertebrates fail, or biases with a different psychometric form, would weaken it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Similar biases can come from different mechanisms.

The published overlaps cover a few paradigms, not the vertebrate illusion battery.

Ant and slime-mold choice data sit in individual papers, not a public trial archive.
